bibl.title: Deep Neural Networks Based Recognition of Plant Diseases by Leaf Image Classification

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: leaf images of 13 visually diagnosable plant diseases, plus healthy leaves and backgrounds, classified by a deep convolutional network
span.quote: The developed model is able to recognize 13 different types of plant diseases out of healthy leaves, with the ability to distinguish plant leaves from their surroundings.

span.label: whether a deep convolutional network trained on internet-sourced leaf images can recognise plant diseases and separate leaves from their surroundings
span.quote: This paper is concerned with a new approach to the development of plant disease recognition model, based on leaf image classification, by the use of deep convolutional networks.

span.label: a CNN plant-disease classifier over a purpose-built 30,880-image augmented database, reaching 96.3% overall, with the whole pipeline described from image collection to fine-tuning
span.quote: New plant disease image database was created, containing more than 3,000 original images taken from the available Internet sources and extended to more than 30,000 using appropriate transformations.

span.label: method
span.quote: This paper is concerned with a new approach to the development of plant disease recognition model, based on leaf image classification, by the use of deep convolutional networks.

span.label: plant disease spreading into regions with no local diagnostic expertise, while misapplied pesticide breeds resistance
span.quote: New diseases can occur in places where they were previously unidentified and, inherently, where there is no local expertise to combat them

span.label: images downloaded from the internet in five languages, deduplicated by metadata and expert-assessed, augmented by affine, perspective and rotation transforms, trained in Caffe, evaluated by 10-fold cross validation
span.term: images downloaded from the internet in five languages, deduplicated by metadata and expert-assessed, augmented by affine, perspective and rotation transforms, trained in Caffe, evaluated by 10-fold cross validation
span.quote: All the images collected for the dataset were downloaded from the Internet, searched by disease and plant name on various sources in different languages, such as Latin, English, German, Serbian, and Hungarian.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: AUGMENTATION SUBSTITUTES FOR DATA: more transformed copies increase the chance the network learns the distinguishing features, and the distortion itself is what reduces overfitting - so the transforms are doing two jobs, enlarging the set and regularising it
span.quote: The main purpose of applying augmentation is to increase the dataset and introduce slight distortion to the images which helps in reducing overfitting during the training stage.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE TRANSFORMS WERE CHOSEN TO MATCH THE DEPLOYMENT: affine, perspective and rotation, because a leaf photographed in a natural environment varies in visual perspective. The augmentation encodes an assumption about how the model will be used, not a generic regulariser
span.quote: The process of augmentation was chosen to fit the needs; the leaves in a natural environment could vary in visual perspective.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A BACKGROUND CLASS TEACHES THE NETWORK WHAT IS NOT A LEAF, taken from the Stanford background dataset - which is why the model can separate leaves from their surroundings at all, and why its best class score (98.21%) is background
span.quote: An extra class in the dataset with background images was beneficial to get more accurate classification. Thus, deep neural network could be trained to differentiate the leaves from the surrounding.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: AUGMENTATION MATTERED MORE THAN FINE-TUNING: fine-tuning moved overall accuracy from 95.8% to 96.3% and is called insignificant by the authors, while augmentation is credited with the result
span.quote: Fine-tuning has not shown significant changes in the overall accuracy, but augmentation process had greater influence to achieve respectable results.

span.label: the no-augmentation baseline was deliberately not explored, so the effect the authors attribute to augmentation is asserted rather than measured
span.quote: As it is known that convolutional networks are able to learn features when trained on larger datasets, results achieved when trained with only original images will not be explored.

span.label: no comparison with other work was possible: the image database was built for this study and the authors say no prior deep-learning work existed in the field
span.quote: Taking into account the fact that during this research our own image database was developed, no one has used it up to now. In addition, since no one has used deep learning to identify plant diseases in scientific literature, it is impossible to compare it with other examples.

span.label: the same point restated in the conclusions - there was no comparison with related results using the exact technique
span.quote: As the presented method has not been exploited, as far as we know, in the field of plant disease recognition, there was no comparison with related results, using the exact technique.

span.label: accuracy was lower for the classes with fewest training images, which the authors name individually
span.quote: From the results displayed in Figure 8, it is notable that the trained model’s accuracy was slightly less for classes with lower number of images in the training dataset, more specifically classes peach, powdery mildew, apple, powdery mildew, and grapevine, wilt.

span.label: the scope is bounded to diseases that can be visually diagnosed from a leaf, which is a property of the photograph rather than of the disease
span.quote: The developed model was able to detect leaf presence and distinguish between healthy leaves and 13 different diseases, which can be visually diagnosed.

span.label: images were downloaded from unspecified internet sources in five languages, so provenance and imaging conditions are uncontrolled
span.quote: All the images collected for the dataset were downloaded from the Internet, searched by disease and plant name on various sources in different languages, such as Latin, English, German, Serbian, and Hungarian.

span.label: duplicate removal compared only file metadata - name, size and date - so two copies of one photograph stored differently would survive the automated pass
span.quote: In this stage, all duplicated images taken from different sources were removed by developed python script applying the comparing procedure. The script removed the duplicates by comparing the images’ metadata: name, size, and the date.

span.label: the authors describe the field itself as lacking, with no commercial solutions beyond species recognition
span.quote: There are many methods in automated or computer vision plant disease detection and classification process, but still, this research field is lacking.

span.label: duplicates were removed by script on image metadata (name, size, date) and the remaining images were then assessed by human experts over several iterations
span.note: eliminates: the same photograph appearing in both training and validation under different filenames - though only partly, since the automated pass compares file metadata rather than image content and the real guard is the expert review · outcome: partial
span.quote: In this stage, all duplicated images taken from different sources were removed by developed python script applying the comparing procedure. The script removed the duplicates by comparing the images’ metadata: name, size, and the date.

span.label: 10-fold cross validation, repeated after every thousand training iterations rather than once at the end
span.note: eliminates: a single fortunate train/test split as the explanation of the accuracy - 10-fold cross validation, repeated every thousand iterations rather than once at the end · outcome: held
span.quote: For the accuracy test, 10-fold cross validation technique was used to evaluate a predictive model. The cross validation procedure was repeated after every thousand training iteration.

span.label: a background class from the Stanford background dataset was added so the network must learn what is not a leaf
span.note: eliminates: the network scoring well by keying on background rather than on the leaf - a background class forces it to learn what is not a leaf, and the 98.21% on that class is what makes the leaf/surroundings separation checkable · outcome: held
span.quote: An extra class in the dataset with background images was beneficial to get more accurate classification. Thus, deep neural network could be trained to differentiate the leaves from the surrounding.

span.label: THE NO-AUGMENTATION BASELINE WAS NOT RUN. The authors state that results from training on original images only `will not be explored`, so the contribution they attribute to augmentation has no control condition
span.note: eliminates: the augmentation itself - training on the original images alone is the comparison that would say how much the augmentation contributed, and the paper states it `will not be explored` · outcome: absent-declared-unreported · would have ruled out, had it been run: nothing - THE CONTROL WAS NOT RUN. The authors state the original-images-only condition `will not be explored`, so the effect attributed to augmentation has no baseline to be measured against
span.quote: As it is known that convolutional networks are able to learn features when trained on larger datasets, results achieved when trained with only original images will not be explored.

span.label: convolutional networks
span.quote: This paper is concerned with a new approach to the development of plant disease recognition model, based on leaf image classification, by the use of deep convolutional networks.

span.label: augmentation
span.quote: The main purpose of applying augmentation is to increase the dataset and introduce slight distortion to the images which helps in reducing overfitting during the training stage.

span.label: overfitting
span.quote: In machine learning, as well as in statistics, overfitting appears when a statistical model describes random noise or error rather than underlying relationship

span.label: affine transformation
span.quote: The image augmentation contained one of several transformation techniques including affine transformation, perspective transformation, and simple image rotations.

span.label: perspective transformation
span.quote: The image augmentation contained one of several transformation techniques including affine transformation, perspective transformation, and simple image rotations.

span.label: cross validation
span.quote: For the accuracy test, 10-fold cross validation technique was used to evaluate a predictive model. The cross validation procedure was repeated after every thousand training iteration.

span.label: fine-tuning
span.quote: After fine-tuning the parameters of the network, an overall accuracy of 96.3% was achieved, after the 100th training iteration (95.8% without fine-tuning).

span.label: precision agriculture
span.quote: Timely and accurate diagnosis of plant diseases is one of the pillars of precision agriculture

span.label: Caffe
span.quote: Caffe, a deep learning framework developed by Berkley Vision and Learning Centre, was used to perform the deep CNN training.

span.label: background images
span.quote: An extra class in the dataset with background images was beneficial to get more accurate classification. Thus, deep neural network could be trained to differentiate the leaves from the surrounding.

span.label: the number of training images in a class → the model's accuracy on that class
span.note: REPORTED AS AN OBSERVED PATTERN ACROSS CLASSES, not as a manipulated effect: accuracy `was slightly less for classes with lower number of images in the training dataset`. Nothing was varied deliberately, so `causes` would assert an experiment the paper did not run - see Q-879. It is also the most useful thing in the results for anyone reusing the model.
span.quote: From the results displayed in Figure 8, it is notable that the trained model’s accuracy was slightly less for classes with lower number of images in the training dataset, more specifically classes peach, powdery mildew, apple, powdery mildew, and grapevine, wilt.

span.label: the 30,880 images - NOT 30,880 PLANTS. Just over 3,000 ORIGINAL images were collected and extended to more than 30,000 by affine, perspective and rotation transforms. Every accuracy figure in the paper rests on a dataset that is roughly 90% transformed copies, and the paper says so plainly
span.quote: New plant disease image database was created, containing more than 3,000 original images taken from the available Internet sources and extended to more than 30,000 using appropriate transformations.

span.label: validation here is 2,589 ORIGINAL images against training on the full 30,880 - so the held-out set is untransformed while training is mostly augmented. THE PAPER DOES NOT STATE WHETHER AUGMENTED COPIES OF THE VALIDATION ORIGINALS WERE EXCLUDED FROM TRAINING, which is the question a reader of the 96.3% would want answered and it is an ABSENCE, not a stated flaw
span.quote: Different tests were performed with 2589 original images, when trained with 30880 images from database.

span.label: `13 different types of plant diseases` - BOUNDED TO WHAT IS VISUALLY DIAGNOSABLE FROM A LEAF. The scope is set by what a photograph of a leaf can show, not by what matters agronomically, and the authors state that bound
span.quote: The developed model was able to detect leaf presence and distinguish between healthy leaves and 13 different diseases, which can be visually diagnosed.

span.label: duplicate removal - BY METADATA ONLY: name, size and date, by script, then human assessment. Two copies of one photograph saved under different names and sizes would survive the automated pass, and the paper's guard against that is the expert review rather than image comparison
span.quote: In this stage, all duplicated images taken from different sources were removed by developed python script applying the comparing procedure. The script removed the duplicates by comparing the images’ metadata: name, size, and the date.

span.label: distinguishes-from → Leafsnap, the existing commercial leaf-image system, which identifies tree SPECIES rather than diseases and was therefore not used as a comparison
span.quote: Presently, there is a commercial solution, Leafsnap \[57\], which uses visual recognition in order to identify tree species from their leaves’ images but as the network presented in this paper is classifying the plant diseases instead of types of plant, Leafsnap was not used for comparison of the achieved results.

span.label: extends → earlier non-deep-learning methods of detecting disease from leaf images, against which the authors say their results are better
span.quote: As the presented method has not been exploited, as far as we know, in the field of plant disease recognition, there was no comparison with related results, using the exact technique.

span.label: augmentation —causes→ overfitting
span.note: direction on the measure: reduces · strength of the relation: 0.9
span.quote: The main purpose of applying augmentation is to increase the dataset and introduce slight distortion to the images which helps in reducing overfitting during the training stage.

span.label: affine transformation —operationalised-as→ augmentation
span.quote: The image augmentation contained one of several transformation techniques including affine transformation, perspective transformation, and simple image rotations.

span.label: background images —operationalised-as→ convolutional networks
span.quote: An extra class in the dataset with background images was beneficial to get more accurate classification. Thus, deep neural network could be trained to differentiate the leaves from the surrounding.

span.label: overall accuracy 96.3% after fine-tuning, 95.8% without; top-5 success 99.99%
span.quote: After fine-tuning the parameters of the network, an overall accuracy of 96.3% was achieved, after the 100th training iteration (95.8% without fine-tuning).

span.label: per-class accuracy ranged from 91.11% (peach powdery mildew) to 98.21% (background images)
span.quote: Achieved accuracy was in range from 91.11% for peach, powdery mildew, up to 98.21% for background images.

span.label: augmentation had a greater influence on the result than fine-tuning, which the authors call insignificant for overall accuracy
span.quote: Fine-tuning has not shown significant changes in the overall accuracy, but augmentation process had greater influence to achieve respectable results.

span.label: high accuracy on background images is what lets the model separate leaves from their surroundings
span.quote: High accuracy of model’s prediction of background images allows good separation of plants leaves and the surroundings.

span.label: overfitting
span.quote: In machine learning, as well as in statistics, overfitting appears when a statistical model describes random noise or error rather than underlying relationship

span.label: augmentation
span.quote: The main purpose of applying augmentation is to increase the dataset and introduce slight distortion to the images which helps in reducing overfitting during the training stage.

span.label: 30,880 training images and 2,589 validation images — None
span.quote: Finally, a database containing 30880 images for training and 2589 images for validation has been created.

span.label: more than 3,000 original images extended to more than 30,000 by transformation — None
span.quote: New plant disease image database was created, containing more than 3,000 original images taken from the available Internet sources and extended to more than 30,000 using appropriate transformations.

span.label: 15 classes - 13 diseases, healthy leaves, and background — None
span.quote: Images in the dataset were grouped into fifteen different classes. Thirteen classes represented plant diseases which could be visually determined from leaves.

span.label: top-1 96.3% and top-5 99.99% after 100,000 iterations — None
span.quote: Top-1 success was 96.3% and top-5 success was 99.99% after 100,000 iterations

span.label: 10-fold cross validation repeated after every thousand training iterations
span.quote: For the accuracy test, 10-fold cross validation technique was used to evaluate a predictive model. The cross validation procedure was repeated after every thousand training iteration.

span.label: number of original training images per class
span.term: number of original training images per class
span.quote: From the results displayed in Figure 8, it is notable that the trained model’s accuracy was slightly less for classes with lower number of images in the training dataset, more specifically classes peach, powdery mildew, apple, powdery mildew, and grapevine, wilt.

span.label: transformation family applied in augmentation - affine, perspective, rotation
span.term: transformation family applied in augmentation - affine, perspective, rotation
span.quote: The image augmentation contained one of several transformation techniques including affine transformation, perspective transformation, and simple image rotations.
